【3】**3.5.3 Summarv**

【4】**Presenting symptoms of MSA are autonomic nervous system， cerebellar， and dysarthric disorders. They may also suffer from REM sleep behavioral disor-der. However， MSA patients only show subtle deficits in cognitive function-ing. In more detail， MSA patients tend to perform worse during the FAB motor scores that assess disinhibition and cognitive flexibility.MSA patients may also be impaired in tests of cognitive speed and in ventral visuopercep-tive tasks. Moreover most investigations comparing PD and MSA patients report a higher amount of depressive mood in MSA patients. Therefore anamnesis and assessment should focus on autonomous nervous system dis-orders， signs of cerebellar dysfunction， motor disinhibition， mood， and word fluency impairments.**

【5】**If the diagnosis is unclear， parts of the assessment (at least 3 minutes) should be performed upright as MSA patients may show hypotension and**

【6】**develop dizziness during that period. In patients early in their disease course and already severely cognitively impaired other diagnosis than MSA should be considered.**

【7】**3.6Visuoperceptive， visuoconstructive impairments， and visual hallucinations in typical and atypical Parkinson's syndromes**

【8】**We can summarize this chapter by stating that visual hallucinations and delusional misidentifications are a characteristic feature of LBD (and PD)； patients with LBD have severe visuoperceptive problems and tend to neglect global configurational patterns which results in increased false positives to small features of spatial configurations. PD patients undergo similar pro-blems， however， to a lesser extent than LBD patients. Hence suffering from visual hallucinationsSand visuoperceptive impairments correlate in these patient groups. This suggests either a common cause for both symptoms or causation of one symptom for the other. A combination of visuoperceptive impairment and decline of EF could be a prominent explanation for the risk of developing visual hallucinations in PD (Santangelo et al.， 2007).**

【9】**However， atypical PD patients， those suffering from PSP or CBD， can also disclose severe impairments with respect to EFs. Yet these atypical PD patients usually do not hallucinate. Moreover these patients have visuoper-ceptive impairments. Fiorenzato et al. (2019) compared 35 PSP patients with Richardson'ssyndrome with130 MSA PD patients. Fiorenzato et al. (2019) followed up about one-half of these groups for a period of 188 months and found that PSP patients were more globally impaired in neuropsychological tests (Montreal Cognitive Assessment， word fluency tasks， Stroop test) as well as in visuoperceptive tasks. The follow-up showed that EFs and judgment of line orientation declined faster in PSP patients than in PD and MSA patients， however， the impairment regarding the incomplete letters test of the VOSP was stable. This would argue that other visuoperceptive tests are related to disease progression in PSP patients as well as in LBD and PD patients. This is especially true for the two latter diseases because LBD and PD patients tend to hallucinate.**

【10】**Bak， Caine， Hearn， and Hodges (2006) compared MSA， PSP， and CBD patients with healthy controls using subtests from the VOSP. CBD/CBS patientsSwere impaired in all VOSP subtests. Patientswith PSP were impaired in number location， dot counting， and silhouette naming. Patients with MSA were not impaired in any of the tests. Ideomotor apraxia， a highly sensitive and specific symptom of CBD/CBS， can be caused by a storage dis-order for the meaning of gestures or action. However， ideomotor apraxia can also be a consequence of a visuoperceptive disorder. This is always the case if the testing comprises meaningless hand positions. During this task， the**

【11】**visual processing of the hand position of the examiner has to be transformed into the proper visuospatial position of the patient’s hand. If the visuospatial matching of visual to motor coordinates is no longer possible， the patient will fail in this task. Thus visuoconstructive impairments are characteristic features of CBD/CBS patients.**

【12】**Going back to the series of studies published by Mori et al. (2000)， Uchiyama et al. (2012)， and Yokoi et al. (2014)， we can see that in LBD patients visual impairment concerns size and form discrimination and over-lapping figures from the BORB (Mori et al.， 2000； Yokoi et al.， 2014)， object decision from the VOSP (Calderon et al.， 2001)， andface recognition(Uchiyama et al.， 2012； Yokoi et al.， 2014) but only inconsistently position discrimination and dot counting (Calderon et al.， 2001； Mori et al.， 2000； Yokoi et al.， 2014). Moreover LBD patients have difficulties responding to local features of figural configurations and not so much to the global features(Barrett et al.， 2001； Uchiyama et al.， 2012； Yokoi et al.， 2014). On the other hand， organizing the different subtests according to the percentage of impaired patients from the Bak et al. (2006) study， clarifies that the impair-ments of PSP and CBD/CBS patients predominantly involve the dot count-ing， the number location， and the cubes tasks from the VOSP. Thus patients with PD or LBD seem to be impaired in visuoperceptive tasks concerning object perception， whereas PSP and CBD/CBS patients seem to be impaired in visuoperceptive tasks concerning object localization and matching spatial coordinate systems of vision and action. Patients with CBD/CBS are often impaired in sensory discrimination and show signs of optic ataxia. Optic ataxia refers to the inability to use visual information to sufficiently guide the hand in the direction of the objects during grasping tasks (Jellinger et al.，2011； Mendez， 2000； Rajagopal， Bateman， & Van Stavern， 2012)， that is， a task for testing object location.**

【13】**Patients with semantic dementia (SD) also show visuoperceptive impair-ments with the core symptom of visual object agnosia. These patients have problems identifying objects， however， they do not suffer from problems in copying them. The explanation for visual object agnosia in these patients may differ from that of patients suffering from classical visual agnostic. Classical visual agnosia is most likely due to a disconnection between visual perception and the stored meaning of objects， whereby the latter is， at least partly， attributable to a degeneration of neuronal repertoires storing the meaning. Furthermore patients with SD do not hallucinate during the early and middle stage of their disease. SD is related to left anterior temporal lobe atrophy. A study from Chan et al. (2009) that compared patients with similar right temporal lobe atrophy with SD patients， revealed that the former patient groups sometimes presented visual hallucination and more behavioral disor-ders. However， one problem with this study was that the right temporal lobe patient groups was selected based on abnormal MRI scans and the amount of**

【14】**atrophy was significantly higher than in the semantic demented group. Therefore the somewhat increased risk of visual hallucination may be caused by more focal atrophy or due to a later stage of the disease progress.**

【15】**Posterior cortical atrophy (PCA) is a visual variant of AD starting with visual impairment and is defined by atrophy in the parietal， occipital， and posterior temporal cortex. Patients suffering from PCA show severe visuo-spatial impairment in a variety of tests. As a result， distinguishing PCA patients from CBD/CBS patients is sometimes difficult， especially in the early phase of their disease. Compared to LBD patients， the visual impairment of PCA starts earlier in the visual processing pathway (Metzler-Baddeley， Baddeley， Lovell， Laffan， & Jones， 2010). Visual hallucinations， however， are rare in patients with PCA and it has， therefore， been proposed that the existence of visual hallucinations contradicts the diagnosis of a pure PCA (Crutch et al.， 2017).**

【16】**When summarizing these different patterns of impairment， it should be clear that visual hallucination cannot be caused primarily by EFs (if that would be the case， PSP and CBD/CBS patients should exhibit even more hallucinations than PD and LBD patients). Additionally， visual hallucinations cannot be caused by any combination of executive impairments and visuo-perceptive processing deficits (in this case visual hallucination should be present in patients with SD and with CBD/CBS). On the other hand， visuo-perceptive deficits alone do not lead to visual hallucinations. Otherwise， visual hallucinations should be a presenting sign of PCA. Thus the specific pattern of visuoperceptive impairments plays a central role in instigating hal-lucinations in patients. Further EF deficits are also a necessary， however， no sufficient condition for developing visual hallucinations.**

【17】**Structural MRI scanning revealed different dominant atrophy patterns in PSP and CBD/CBS patients when compared to LBD patients. Bozzali et al.(2005) used diffusion tensor imaging in 15 patients with LBD and mild dementia. They discovered a correlation between white matter dysfunction in the occipitotemporal lobe and VOSP “incomplete letter” performance. Gallagher et al. (2011) counted postmortem Lewy bodies in different regions of the brain and compared the density of Lewy body counts with the exis-tence of visual hallucinations. According to Gallagher et al.， a correlation for the middle frontal， the middle temporal gyri， transentorhinal and the anterior cingulate cortices is present， however no such correlation exists for the parie-tal cortex. They argue that visual hallucination might be the result of frontal EF dysfunctions (loss of cognitive control) and a higher order temporal lobe based visual perceptive impairment. On the other hand， in SD atrophy is con-centrated in the anterior temporal cortex and not in the posterior or occipito-temporal cortex.**

【18】**In LBD/PD the ventral pathway (vision for object identification) seems to be more impaired than the dorsal pathway. Consequently， it can be stated， that visual hallucinations rely on a combination of disorders in the ventral visual pathway and in EFs. A combination of abnormal processing in the dorsal pathway with executive impairments does not cause visual hallucina-tions， as shown by PSP and CBD/CBS. Moreover the ventral processing impairment must be located in early stages of this pathway where the input is not already abstracted from its visual features. Otherwise， SD patients would also hallucinate.**

【19】**What does that mean for clinical routine and neuropsychological differen-tial diagnosing?**

【20】**1\. Atypical Parkinson's syndromes like PSP and CBD/CBS may suffer from visuoperceptive disorders， especially in visuoconstructive and visuospa-tial tests， and not so much in visuoperceptive tasks assessing vision for object recognition. This combination would argue for an impairment in the dorsal visual stream， that is， in the “where” path of visual analysis. For LBD and PD， the opposite pattern is the case， that is， an impairment of the ventral pathway. Neuropsychological testing should therefore involve visuoperceptive tests for both visual pathways if the diagnosis is unclear. These additional tests should be able to dissociate performance between these two pathways.**

【21】**_2\._ Typical PD patients usually do not suffer from low-level dorsal stream impairments like optic ataxia or ideomotor apraxia. Therefore any prob-lem in this domain should always be a red flag for the diagnosis of an alphasynucleinopathic disease.**

【22】**3\. Neurodegenerative patients suffering from visual object agnosia without clear visuoconstructive impairments often suffer from SD， but not from LBD/PD or CBD/CBS/PD.**

【73】**INTRODUCTION**

【74】Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a low-grade lympho-proliferative disorder of mature (peripheral) lymphoid B cells characterized by lymphocytosis， CD5/CD23 coexpression

【75】**and involvement of the blood， bone marrow (BM)， spleen， and lymph nodes \[1-6\]. In the absence of extramedullary tis-sue involvement， to diagnose CLL there must be 25×109L monoclonal lymphocytes with a CLL phenotype in the blood for >3 months. A level below this threshold is considered a monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL). The data sug-gest that most patients with CLL go through a prolonged**

【76】**prodromal phase with evidence of circulating clone found many years prior to diagnosis. A recent report suggests that the cut-point between MBL and CLL should be modified and increased to a B-cell count of 11× 10°/L \[7，8\].**

【77】Small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) involving the lymph nodes and extranodal sites， and composed of small lympho-cytes admixed with variable proportion of prolymphocytes and paraimmunoblasts forming characteristic proliferation centers is considered a lymphomatous counterpart of CLL. CLL shows considerable variations in cytomorphologic， immunophenotypic， and prognostic features. Typical CLL， which constitutes approximately 80% of cases， can be defined as having >90% small lymphocytes with weak expression of surface immunoglobulin and CD20， and coexpression of CD5 and CD23. Atypical CLL shows larger lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm， prolymphocytes-like or cleaved cells， and aberrant phenotype.

【78】**The clinical course of CLL ranges from a very indolent disorder with a normal lifespan to a progressive disease with poor prognosis. Patients having aggressive disease require therapy within relatively short time after diagnosis， whereas patients with asymptomatic disease are not likely to ben-efit from palliative chemotherapy. The median survival of patients with CLL is 10 years. Patients with poor prognostic factors have median survival of ~3 years. The course of the disease depends on a number of factors including age， gen-der， Binet/Rai stage， performance status， laboratory param-eters \[lymphocyte count， thymidine kinase， soluble CD23， Bz-microglobulin， lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)\]， atypical cytologic features， pattern and extent of BM infiltration， 17p deletion， TP53 mutation/loss， deletion of chromosome 11q23， ATM status， IGVH mutational status， BIRC3 abnormali-ties， NOTCHI mutational status， SF3BI mutational status， and CD38 and ZAP-70 expression \[9-13\]. The significant improvements in remission rates have been achieved with newer therapeutic approaches including purine analogs (e.g.， fludarabine) in combination with monoclonal antibodies and stem cell transplantation \[14-16\]. The combination of ritux-imab and fludarabine or fludarabine-containing regimens has yielded overall response rates of 95%， with complete response rates up to 66% in previously untreated CLL patients \[17\]. CLL cases refractory to treatment have a very poor progno-sis， despite various salvage therapy strategies \[18-20\]**

【79】**RISK CATEGORIES IN CLL**

【80】**Several risk categories can be distinguished in CLL patients based on the response to treatment， and cytogenetic and molecular changes. In the scheme proposed by Zenz et al.\[12\]， the patients with CLL are divided into highest risk， high risk， and low risk：**

【81】**Highest-risk CLL category includes patients with TP53 loss/mutations， lack of response to purine ana-logs， or very short response (<24 months) to prior treatment with fludarabine， cyclophosphamide， and rituximab. These patients are candidates for drugs**

【82】**with proven activity in TP53-deleted/mutant cells， investigational aagents， and allogeneic stem cell transplantation.**

【83】High-risk CLL includes patients with unmutated IGVH， 11q deletion， and high B-microglobulin.

【84】Low risk includes patients with no prior therapy and lack of the high-risk factors.

【85】**Based on the genetic lesions and cytogenetic analysis of patients with CLL， Rossi et al.\[13\] proposed four CLL prog-nostic groups：**

【86】**1\. High-risk， harboring TP53 and/or BIRC3 abnormal-ities (10-year survival： 29%)**

【87】2\. Intermediate-risk， harboring NOTCHI and/or SFBI mutations and/or del(11q22-23) (10-year survival：37%)

【88】3\. Low-risk， harboring +12 or a normal genetics(10-year survival： 57%)

【89】4\. Very low-risk， harboring del(13q14) only (10-year survival： 69.3%)

【90】**DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA FOR CLI**

【91】The diagnostic criteria for CLL are as follows：

【92】Blood. The diagnosis of CLL requires the presence of25×10°/L B lymphocytes in the blood for the duration of at least 3 months. The clonality of the circulating B cells needs to be confirmed by flow cytometry (FC). The identification of >55% prolymphocytes favors the diagnosis of B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (B-PLL). In the absence of lymphadenopathy or organomegaly， cytopenias， or disease-related symptoms， the presence of <5 × 10°/L B lymphocytes in blood is defined as“monoclonal B lymphocytosis."The cytopenia caused by a typical marrow infiltrate defines the diagnosis of CLL regardless of the number of blood B lymphocytes.

【93】**Immunophenotype. CLL cells express CD5， CD23， and B-cell antigens (CD19， CD20，CD22， CD79a). The expression of CD20 and surface immunoglobu-lins is weak.**

【94】Staging. The two main staging methods that are used in CLL are Rai and Binet systems.

【95】_Other tests performed at diagnosis. With the excep-_ tion of fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)， the application of additional tests at diagnosis should not be used in routine practice to influence therapy and is generally not recommended. However， certain parameters， such as immunoglobulin mutational sta-tus， are useful for predicting the clinical course in individual cases. The following tests should be rec-ommended for patients who want a better prediction of the rate at which their disease might progress：

【100】**MONOCLONAL B-CEll LYMPHOCYTOSIS**

【101】The presence of low numbers (<5 ×10"/L) of circulating monoclonal B cells (overall kappa to lambda ratio >3：1 or<0.3：1) in otherwise healthy subjects (no evidence of CLL/other lymphoproliferative disorders， adenopathy， or organo-megaly) is being recently categorized as MBL \[7，8，21-24\]. When the number of clonal cells is 5×10°/L or more， stage 0CLL is diagnosed. Most MBLs (75%) have the phenotype of CLL with dim CD20 and dim surface immunoglobulin expression， and coexpression of CD5 and CD23 (CLL-like MBL). The remaining MBLs are classified as atypical CLL(CD5+， CD23-， and bright CD20) and CD5-MBL \[8，21\]. The incidence of MBL increased with age， reaching a frequency of >20% in persons aged >60 years and being more frequent among the relatives \[22，25\] of patients with CLL \[26-29\]. CLL-like MBL can further be subdivided into clinical MBL and population-screening MBL. The former is diagnosed in a clinical setting， is associated with lymphocytosis， and has a concentration of clonal B cells >1500/uL. Population-screening MBL is only detected during screening studies of healthy persons in the general population and is character--COUI ized by ≤50 clonal B cells/uL (low-count MBL). Virtually， all patients with CLL had a preceding MBL. The potential risk of progression of clinical MBL (previously termed MBL with lymphocytosis) into clinically overt CLL is ~1.1%per year.

【102】Rawstron et al. \[25\] reported minute monoclonal B-cell populations (<3.5×10"L) with the phenotype of CLL in the blood of 5% of healthy individuals (older than 60 years). Nieto et al. \[22\] analyzed the frequency of circulating mono-clonal B cells in 608 healthy subjects older than 40 years with normal blood count using a highly sensitive multicolor FC and found clonal CLL-like B cells in 12% of patients(0.17±0.13×10°/L). The clinical significance of MBL is uncertain at the moment， and long-term follow-up studies are needed to define its natural history (e.g.， the risk of progres-sion into CLL).

【103】Shanafelt et al.\[7\] analyzed the relationship of absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) and B-cell count with clinical out-come in 459 patients with a clonal population of CLL pheno-type to determine (1) whether the CLL diagnosis should be based on ALC or B-cell count， (2) what lymphocy te threshold should be used for diagnosis， and (3) whether any lympho-cyte count has independent prognostic value after account-ing for biologic/molecular prognostic markers. B-cell count and ALC had similar value for predicting treatment-free survival and overall survival (OS) as continuous variables，

【104】but as binary factors， a B-cell threshold of 11 ×10%L best predicted survival.

【105】Fazi et al. \[24\] evaluated 76 low-count MBLs with five-color FC： 90% CLL-like MBL but only 44.4% atypical CLL and 66.7% CD5-MBL persisted over time. Population-screening CLL-like MBL had no relevant cell count change， and none developed an overt leukemia. In 50% of the cases， FISH showed CLL-related chromosomal abnormalities. including monoallelic or biallelic 13q deletions (43.8%)， tri-somy 12 (one case)， and 17p deletions (two cases).

【106】Clinical MBL is similar in terms of phenotypic and karyotypic/genotypic changes to early CLL and， in contrast to the majority of low-count MBL， may progress into treat-ment-requiring CLL. In both early CLL and clinical MBL， a value of 11 ×10/L appears to be associated with disease progression.

【107】Histologic and immunophenotypic analysis of the BM in patients with MBL shows atypical lymphoid infiltrate in the majority of patients \[30\]. Randen et al. \[30\] reported three infiltration patterns： (1) focal interstitial， (2) nodular(nonparatrabecular)， and (3) discrete diffuse lymphocytosis. Focal interstitial lymphoid infiltrate is seen in patients with CLL-like MBL， whereas the other patterns are not related to a particular MBL phenotype.

【108】**IMMUNOPHENOTYPE OF CLL**

【109】Among B cells， CD38 is expressed at high levels by B-lineage progenitors in BM and by B-lymphocytes in ger-minal center， in activated tonsils， and by terminally differ-entiated plasma cells. In CLL， CD38 expression identifies two subgroups of patients with different clinical outcomes， including OS， time to first treatment， number of leukemic cells with abnormal morphology， extent of adenopathy， ALC， and LDH and B-microglobulin levels. In the majority of studies， the threshold is considered as ≥30% CD38+ clonal cells \[9，32-36\]. At the molecular level， the CD38+ and CD38-clones differ in the level of expression of activation mark-ers CD69 and HLA-DR， Ki-67 fraction， ZAP-70 expression，

Although CD38 expression is associated with mutated CLL， recent reports suggest that combination of CD38 and IGVH mutational status had greater prognostic power than either marker alone \[40，41\].

【112】**MORPHOLOGY Blood and BM Aspirate**

【113】In the BM aspirate and blood smears， CLL cells are small with scanty pale cytoplasm， round nuclei， and clumped (coarse) chromatin (see Figure 8.3). Occasional smudge cells and larger lymphocytes including prolymphocytes and paraim-munoblasts are usually also present. Prolymphocytes are dis-tinguished from small lymphocytes by their relatively larger size， increasingly abundant pale cytoplasm， and prominent central nucleolus (Figure 8.4). Paraimmunoblasts have oval nuclei with large central nucleolus and grayish-blue cyto-plasm. CLL with >15% and <55% prolymphocytes defines B-chronic lymphocytic leukemia/prolymphocytic leukemia(B-CLL/PLL). B-prolymphocytic leukemia (B-PLL) has>55% of prolymphocytes.

【114】**BM Biopsy**

【115】Patterns of BM involvement by CLL include nodular， inter-stitial， and diffuse (Figure 8.5). The infiltrate is composed of mostly small lymphocytes with scattered prolymphocytes and paraimmunoblasts. In cases with prominent BM involve-ment， proliferation centers are often present. The presence of large atypical cells should raise the possibility of Richter’s transformation.

【116】Pattern and extent of BM involvement (diffuse vs. non-diffuse) have prognostic implications \[42\]， although it is not independent of the staging and with novel phenotypic， chromo-somal， and molecular markers， histologic pattern became less relevant \[43\]. Nodular and interstitial patterns are associated with early disease and better

【0】use for the catastrophe. In suspected cases， investiga-tions should include blood analysis for serum glucose， sodium， potassi-um， calcium， phosphorus， magnesium，BUN， pH and blood gas analysis， urinalysis， microbiological tests as dictated by the merits of the case， ECG monitoring， EEG， barium swallow， esophageal pH studies， chest X-ray and skeletal survey and 4 to 8 hour sleep studies.

【1】Apnea of 20 seconds or more is significant. It may be of three types：

【2】1\. Central as a result of absent neurological output from the res-piratory center，

【3】2\. Obstructive as a result of closure of the upper airway (even lower airway may be involved) so that the infant fails to experi-ence airflow despite considerable respiratory effort，

【4】3\. Mixed as result of combination of an obstructive episode and cen-tral apnea. Though， apnea has been incriminated in the etiology of SIDS， the cause and effect relationship remains unclear.

【5】Anatomical and developmentalanomalies of the upper airway may cause obstruction and， perhaps， SIDS or ALTE， e.g. posterior displacement of the tongue as in Pierre Robin syndrome， reduced airway diameter following neck flexion， cleft palate， laryngo-malacia， tracheomalacia， bronchomalacia， laryngeal cleft or other anomalies， tracheoesophageal fistula of H-type，

【6】bronchomalacia， vascular rings， immature or abnormal neuromus-cular control of oropharyngeal muscles， etc. In the presence of a viral respiratory infection， proneness to airway obstruction may be enhanced.

【7】Introduction of some fluids into the larynx may stimulate reflex apnea and reflux with aspiration， and cause SIDS.

【8】**Cardiac Anomalies (Arrhythmias)**

【9】The role of cardiac arrhythmias (R on T phenomenon， sick sinus syndrome) in the causation of SIDS remains debatable. No significant difference in cardiac rhythm is found between infants dying of SIDS and the normal controls. In ALTE， a proportion of the infants exhibit increased vagal tone. The resultant bradycardia is， perhaps，triggered by events such as a reflux.

【10】**Gastroesophageal Reflux**

【11】Reflux， a common finding in first 6 months of life， has been shown to produce apnea in some studies. How far it contributes to occur-rence of SIDS remains unclear.

【12】Abnormality in autonomic nervous system in infants with ALTE is evidenced by increased heart rate， and decreased heart-rate viability， shorter QT index and higher ventilatory response to CO，.

【13】In SIDS， increased levels of dopamine in carotid bodies are found. In infants with abnormal autonomic nervous system， a relationship be-tween SIDS and short-chain opioid peptides， e.g. B-casomor-phine， has been postulated.

【14】The role of such chemical mediators as catecholamines， endor-phins， and serotonin in causation of SIDS has also been speculat-ed.

【15】**Brainstem and Carotid Body Defects**

【16】Evidence suggests that brainstem and carotid body defects may be responsible for some cases of SIDS. The former circuit controls res-piratory or cardiac stability. The integrity of the latter is important for oxygen responsiveness as also sheer survival.

【32】**Familial Tall Stature**

【33】This kind of tallness can be recognized from the family history indicat-ing that the child is taking after one or other parent or a close relative. The child is born with an above-average length. During all stages of growth， he shows a proportionate but above-average growth.

【34】**Marfan's Syndrome**

【35】This autosomal dominant disease is characterized by tall stature with strikingly low upper segment-lower segment ratio， arm span > height and long slender bones of forearm and long metacarpals together with multiple skeletal， cardiovascular and ocular malformations (Figs 59.1and 59.2). Tallness and slimness are frequently seen right at birth and persist postnatally. Now two types of the condition are recognized：infantile (congenital) and adult (Table 59.2).

【40】**Tall Stature**

【41】**Klinefelter's Syndrome**

【42】This 47， XXY syndrome is characterized by， besides tallness， frank mental retardation or simply psychosocial，learning or school adjustment problems， slimness， long legs， poor weight， underdeveloped testes and phalus and delayed pubertal development. All tall boys， more so with mental retardation， must have karyop-typing to exclude Klinefelter's syndrome.

【43】**Cerebral Gigantism**

【44】Also termed Sotos syndrome or primordial gigantism， in this condition rapid linear growth occurs during the first 4 years so that the child reaches 97th percentile from the birth length of over 90th percentile. Additional features include large hands and feet， a large head， anti-mongoloid slant (down-slanting eyes)， a high-arched palate and men-tal retardation. A non-progressive hypothalamic lesion is blamed for this disorder.

【48】The term， vertigo (Latin， meaning "turning round")， denotes the sensa-tion of moving around in space or having objects move about the person. The former is termed subjective vertigo and the latter objective vertigo.

【49】Itiscoften， though wrongly， employed for dizziness， light-head-edness or giddiness.

【50】History should include time of onset of vertigo， presence or absence of preceding aura， relationship with meals， etc. Any preceding illness， especially in relation to the ears， trauma or drug intake. Any accompa-nying symptoms such as headache， hearing loss， tinnitus， nausea vom-iting， nystagmus or visual complaint? Any psychosocial problem(s)? Any suggestion of hyperventilation?

【51】Physical examination， over and above GPE， should focus on ENT， CNS and psychosocial evaluation. It is important to look for anemia in particular and record blood pressure.

【52】Severe shock or fright may set a neurogenic mechanism (vasovagal stimulation)， causing syncope and vertigo.

【62】Symptoms， in addition to vertigo， include tachypnea， tachycardia， diaphoresis， generalized weakness， fainting and seizures.

【63】**Epidemic Vertigo**

【64】The condition follows an upper respiratory infection (viral). It occurs in recurrences and subsides in a matter of a week or two.

【65】**Benign Paroxysmal Vertigo**

【66】Occuring at 1-3 years of age， a suddent attack of severe vertigo may be accompanied by vomiting and nystagmus. The terrified child becomes pale， sweats profusel， cries and clings to mother. The attack lasts a some seconds or minutes but recurrences may be seenover months and sometimes years. In contrast to epilepsy， sensorium is preserved. The condition may well be a migraine equivalent.

【80】Vomiting， a common symptom during infancy and childhood， is de-fined as forcible expulsion of contents of the stomach from the mouth. The strong contraction of the muscles of the abdominal wall and vi-olent descent of diaphragm is the triggering factor that operates in its causation， irrespective of the actual cause.

【81】The vomiting center lies in the cerebral medulla. Since it is under influence of chemoreceptors， disease affecting nearly any system-of course， brain is the most important-may cause vomiting. An obstructive lesion at pylorus or beyond， for instance， may cause vomiting by vis-ceral afferents reaching the vomiting center.

【82】History-taking should pay special attention to the age of the child who vomits. Vomiting in the newborn infant may have altogether different implications than vomiting in later infancy and childhood. For instance， it is normal for a neonate to bring up small amounts of feed without being adversely affected as far as his health and well-being are concerned. Such vomiting， howsoever minor， in a young child should arouse suspicion of some organic problem.

【83】It is of value to determine precisely its frequency and whether the problem is acute or it had been there in a recurrent form over quite a few months. What is the amount， color and character of vomitus? Any relationship with feeding? Any abdominal discomfort or pain? Any accompanying drooling? Any suggestion of food poisoning? Does the child have associated diarrhea and dehydration? Any weight loss? Any convulsions， drowsiness or unconsciousness? Is there any history of trauma， especially to the head?

【84】**Vomiting**

【85】Physical examination should ascertain the hydration and nutri-tional status of the child. Any evidence of infection? Any neurolog-ic abnormality?

【86】**VOMITING IN THE NEWBORN**

【87】**Benign**

【88】Swallowed amniotic fluid or blood may be responsible for vomiting in a few days after birth. Though the symptom causes much anxiety， it settles down in due course without any treatment.

【89】Swallowed air due to erratic feeding， say far-too-rapid feeding or feeding a very large amount in a short time， is a common cause of vom-iting or regurgitation in the newborn and early infancy. The vomitus is unchanged， contains no curd and is not maladrous. Vomiting in such cases occurs either soon after the feed or sometime within an hour's time. These babies with erratic feeding also suffer frequently from abdominal distention and colic. Accompanying these manifestations may be failure to thrive.

【90】The common causes of organic vomiting in the newborn are sep-ticemia and other infections such as meningitis， intrauterine infec-tions causing encephalitis， otitis， gastroenteritis， and congenital ob-structive defects of the gastrointestinal tract. The remaining causes include birth trauma， birth defects of CNS， hypoglycemia and galactosemia.

【91】The organic cause of vomiting should be considered in the pres-ence of the following features：

【92】1\. Persistent vomiting despite correction of feeding technique 2. Accompanying abdominal distention 3.

【93】Green vomitus which should be regarded as due to intestinal obstruction until and unless proved otherwise 4.

【100】Septicemia： Vomiting may be the earliest symptom of this serious neonatal problem. Remaining manifestations include lethargy， refusal of feed， irritability， restlessness， loose motions， abdominal distention， fever or hypothermia， failure to gain weight， jaundice， respiratory dis-tress and skin eruptions. Umbilicus is often septic. Hepatosplenomegaly and pallor may accompany the clinical picture. Occurrence of seizures should arouse suspicion of meningitis.

【101】_Meningitis：Vomiting may well be the only manifestation of_ meningitis during neonatal period. Drowsiness， poor feeding and convulsions may occur later. Bulging anterior fontanel may or may not occur. Neck stiffness is seldom present. In view of great emer-gency involved in the diagnosis and treatment of this condition， it is important that lumbar puncture is done immediately.

【102】Hirschsprung disease： Vomiting together with abdominal distention and failure to pass stools during the first week of life may suggest the diagnosis of this condition. Following rectal examination， the baby may have relief from these symptoms. Explosive discharge of feces and gas is characteristic. Episodes of constipation alternating with diarrhea， failure to gain weight and even weight loss， dehydration， hypoproteinemia and edema are some of the other manifestations of this disorder.

【112】Esophageal atresia： In the most common type， esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula， the baby regurgitates and vomits all feeds and his mouth overflows with mucus and saliva. There is history of his having choked and vomited on his very first feed. Profuse chocking， coughing， cyanosis， excessive drooling and abdominal disten-tion are frequent.

【113】Diagnosis is established by demonstrating air in the stomach and intestines in the plain X-ray abdomen.

【114】Alternatively， you may introduce a catheter down the infant's esopha-gus and take a X-ray film. In case of atresia， the catheter gets coiled in the blind upper pouch as seen in the plain X-ray film. You may intro-duce a small amount of diluted barium to confirm the diagnosis.

【115】Since incidence of maternal hydramnios in such babies is high， it is a good practice to rule out the presence of esophageal atresia before giv-ing feed to the baby， born to a mother with hydramnios.

【116】_Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis： Vomiting， starting in the_ second half of the first month and progressively becoming forceful and projectile within 30 minutes of feeding， constant hunger and failure to thrive are classical manifestations of this condition. Occasionally， greenish stools (starvation diarrhea)， gastric hemorrhage or jaundice may be present. Dehydration， electrolyte imbalance-especially alkalosis， hypokalemia， hyponatremia and tetany may complicate the picture.

【117】Barium meal study showing gross narrowing and elongation of pylorus， markedly distended stomach with retention of barium and increased in-tensity of peristaltic waves confirm the diagnosis.

Manifestations (as a consequence of excessive reflux of the stom-ach contents into the esophagus) include vomiting， rumination and failure to thrive. Vomiting characteristically occurs when the baby is returned to the cot (Fig. 61.1).

【29】1\. Monocytes are circulating cells with a halflife of 12-24 hours. They leave the blood stream and enter tissues， differentiating into macrophages ("big eaters") specific for the particular organ (e.g.， alveolar macrophages， splenic macrophages， liver Kupffer cells， brain microglial cells， dendritic cells). They have diverse functions， such as phagocytosis， lymphocyte activation， and other cytokine-mediated activities. Many disorders affecting PMNs， including toxins and infections， also affect monocytes. A significant increase in monocytes， how-ever， should prompt consideration of certain specific conditions.

【30】2\. In the presence of monocytosis， examine for malignancy， tuberculosis， and a few other odd infections.

【49】1.. The normal concentration of neutrophils is approximately 3650/ml (range1830-7250). The absolute neutrophil count ("ANC") is determined by multiply-ing the percent neutrophils by the total white blood cell count. When the ANC is less than 1000， infectious complications increase significantly， and the inflam-matory process is essentially absent when the ANC is less than 200. Neutro-penia may result from four basic mechanisms： autoimmune or antibody-mediated peripheral destruction； neoplastic， infiltrative， or toxic depression of the marrow； cardiopulmonary bypass and hemodialysis； or sepsis/overwhelming infection.

【50】2\. Autoimmune processes may feature antineutrophil antibodies and/or hy-persplenism， causing neutropenia. Examples include SLE， rheumatoid arthritis， Felty's syndrome， ond Wegener’s granulomatosis.. DDrugs such as diuretics5

【51】alpha-methyl dopa， and some phenothiazines also may act as haptens， promot-ing peripheral destruction of neutrophils.

【52】3\. Processes that impair marrow production of neutrophils include neoplastic invasion， infiltrative/infectious involvement of the marrow， and the cytotoxic effects of drugs. Neutropenia is common in patients treated with high doses of chemotherapy. The duration and severily of neutropenia can be ameliorated by administration of G-CSF.

【53】4\. Cardiopulmonary bypass and hemodialysis cause peripheral pooling and a transient neutropenia. Sepsis/overwhelming infections also may cause a transient neutropenia， which may be an effect of endotoxin release. Be careful not to miss sepsis， especially in elderly patients， who may have a paucity of other signs of infection.

【54】5\. Neutropenic patients are predisposed to infections with bacteria and fungi(especially Candida and Aspergillus). Some conditions occurring predominantly in neutropenic patients include skin lesions from fungal infection， ecthyma gan-grenosum (often a result of Pseudomonas infection). Sweet’s syndrome (neu-trophilic dermatosis)， typhlitis (inflammation of the cecum)， perirectal infections， and opportunistic pneumonias.

Neutrophilia， an increase inn "PMNS" (polymorphonuclear neutrophils)， re-sults from four primary processes： peripheral demargination of existing PMNs， marrow release of an existing pool of PMNs， newly synthesized PMNs， and stimulation by miscellaneous systemic diseases (probably by a combination of related processes).

【70】_2\._ . Peripheral demargination occurs when neutrophils outside the bone marrow are released from their sites of adherence along blood vessels (many along vessels in the spleen and lung). This process can rapidly double the number of neutrophils seen on the peripheral smear. Demargination occurs with physiologic stress， exercise， exogenous epinephrine administration， steroid ther-apy， and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents. The deficiency of the leukocyte adhesion protein CR3 causes neutrophils to adhere poorly to endothelial cells and margination is inhibited. Patients with this defect have prominent neu-trophilia and recurrent infections.

【71】3\. Marrow release of an existing pool of neutrophils occurs with steroid ther-apy， acute infections， and inflammation (e.g.， thermal injury).

【72】4\. New synthesis of PMNs occurs in response to infections， necrosis of tissue (e.g.， gangrene， pulmonary or myocardial infarction， thermal injury)， in-flammatory states (e.g.， vvaassccuulliittiiss，， hypersensitivity reactions)， steroid therapy， and myeloproliferative disorders (e.g， polycythemia vera， AML， myeloid metaplasia).

【73】5.Various systemic disorders， including diabetic ketoacidosis， uremia from acute renal failure， metastatic cancers， acute hemorrhage， hemolysis， and eclampsia， can stimulate neutrophilia. Toxic exposures such as poisoning and lithium administration also may be associated with neutrophilia. The mecha-nism of neutrophilia in these disorders may be a combination of the above processes.

【107】There are four primary mechanisms of pancytopenia： aplastic marrow(hypocellular)， invaded marrow (neoplasm， storage diseases)， dysplastic marrow (normo or hypercellular)， and splenomegaly. As the mnemonic suggests， HlV infection should be considered in any patient with pancytopenia.

【108】2\. Causes of aplastic anemia include congenital disorders (e.g.， Fanconi's anemia)， chemical and other toxic exposures (e.g.， benzene， alkylating agents， arsenicals， radiation)， immunologically mediated aplasia (e.g.， SLE)， infections(e.g.， hepatitis， parvovirus)， other miscellaneous associations (e.g.， pregnancy， transfusion-associated graft versusShost disease)， and idiopathic aplastic anemia. Marrow invasion and replacement occurs with hematologic malignan-cies， metastatic cancers， storage cell disorders， osteopetrosis， and myelofibro-sis. Dysplastic disorders feature a normal or hypercellular marrow and include

【109】B12 deficiency，folate deficiency，AIDS，cand primary myelodysplasia. Splenomegaly and consequent hypersplenism promote accelerated removal of cells from circulation， and marrow cellularity is usually normal.

【110】3\. In approaching pancytopenia， first rule out drugs， toxins， infections (e.g.， AlDS)， and nutritional deficiencies as causes. Examination of the peripheral smear may provide clues to the diagnosis， but bone marrow aspiration and biopsy are the definitive tests.

【124】1.TTP is a disease of unknown etiology. The diagnosis is based on the pentad of： (1) renal dysfunction， (2) elevated body temperature， (3) thrombocytopenia，(4) intravascular hemolysis ("microangiopathic")， and (5) central nervous system dysfunction (i.e.， altered mental status， seizures).

【125】2\. TTP may be the result of endothelial release of abnormal Von Willebrand factor multimers. These multimers precipitate the formation of fibrin microthrombi

【126】that occlude blood vessels and damage RBCs and platelets. There is also evi dence that an inhibition or deficiency of a critical Von Willebrand cleaving factor is responsible for the microthrombi. The result is a microangiopathic process with severe thrombocytopenia and anemia. The primary end-organ damage is seen in renal and neurologic dysfunction. The peripheral smear is the key to making a prompt diagnosis and initiating treatment. The smear shows schistocytes， cells damaged by the microangiopathic process， and a marked reticulocytosis("RETIC"). The reticulocytosis is evidence that the marrow is functioning normally in response to peripheral destruction of RBCs. The MCV (see Anemia section) is elevated because of the increase in these large， immature erythrocytes.

【127】3\. Coagulation tests are normal in TTP， whereas in DIC abnormalities of PT， PTT， fibrinogen， fibrin split products， and D-dimer are the rule.

【128】_4\._ Treatment of TTP involves prompt plasmapheresis and plasma exchange. Intravenous immunoglobulin， vincristine， and glucocorticoids may be beneficial， but controlled studies are lacking. Splenectomy may have a role in refractory cases. Platelet transfusions are not indicated.

【129】5\. Hemolytic uremic syndrome， a syndrome closely related to TTP， is seen pre-dominantly in children and has more prominent renal involvement. It may occur after gastroenteritis caused by E. coli 0157：H7

【136】1.. Thrombocytopenia is a result of one of four problems： peripheral destruction， laboratory error， trapping in the spleen， and synthetic problems. Peripheral de struction of platelets occurs with ITP， DIC TTP， PTP， prosthetic valves， pregnancy associated disorders， certain drugs， systemic infections， and collagen vascular diseases. Laboratory error may occur with automated differentials. Be certain to look at the peripheral smear to rule out platelet clumping， which will give a

【137】falsely low count. Trapping in the spleen (sequestration) reduces circulating platelets and is seen in any of the processes that cause splenomegaly (see Splenomegaly section). Synthesis problems are primary bone marrow produc-tion abnormalities that occur with invasion of marrow， drugs (those causing marrow suppression)， and some infections. Synthesis problems also may feature decreased numbers of other cells (see Pancytopenia section).

【138】2\. Acute thrombocytopenia is an emergency， and "ITPS" lists the most important etiologies. A prompt diagnosis is critical， because bleeding can be life-threaten-ing， and the treatments differ.

【139】**ITPS**

【140】Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) Pregnancy/Post-transfusion purpura (PTP) Sepsis/disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)

【141】3\. ITP or immune thrombocytopenia may occur as an isolated phenomenon or in association with malignancies， collagen vascular diseases， or administration of certain drugs. Antibody-mediated destruction of platelets may require im-munosuppressive therapy. A careful search for a causative drug is critical， as small amounts of the offending agent can trigger the reaction. Prolonged throm-bocytopenia occurs with drugs that are cleared slowly from the body， such as gold and phenytoin. Heparin causes a specific and potentially catastrophic syn-drome of thrombocytopenia and arterial thrombosis called heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. The heparin-induced platelet antibody test is diagnostic. All heparin， including lV flushes， must be discontinued.

【142】4\. TTP and the closely related hemolytic uremic syndrome are treated with plasma exchange (see TTP section).

【143】5\. PTP and pregnancy-associated syndromes should be suspected in women with acute thrombocytopenia. PTP is a rare phenomenon that occurs 1 week after transfusion in individuals (almost always women) lacking certain platelet antigens (the most common is PLA1). Most patients have had a prior exposure to PLA1 antigens during pregnancy or a prior transfusion. Intravenous immunoglob-ulin or steroids may facilitate recovery in 4-5 days. The related pregnancy-as-sociated syndromes of eclampsia， acute fatty liver， and HELLP (hemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelets) are life-threatening. Microangiopathic destruction lowers platelets precipitously， and timely delivery of the fetus is the only cure.

【144】6\. Sepsis/DIC is a syndrome of anemia， thrombocytopenia， and coagulopa-thy often occurring in association with a severe， systemic infection. It also occurs in association with malignancies and inflammatory conditions such as pancreatitis.

【145】**■**

【146】Patients have rapidly falling hemoglobins and platelet counts， with an ele-vated partial thromboplastin time. Bleeding and ischemia from clotting may be present. There is a bigh mortality rate， and improvements occur with treat-ment of the underlying illness. There may be some benefit in trying to treat severe bleeding (platelet， RBC， and plasma transfusions) or ischemia (heparin) in certain patients， but such treatment is individualized. Treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia may precipitate DIC， and prophylactic heparin is of benefit.

【147】7.. The approach to thrombocytopenia includes a complete history with a care-ful search for possible causative drugs， infections， or inflammatory conditions， and a physical examination focusing on the spleen and liver. The peripheral blood smear is examined for evidence of clumping， microangiopathic changes， or other abnormalities. If the cause is not certain， then a prompt bone marrow biopsy should be performed. Patients with ITP， TTP， PTP， and other causes of pe ripheral destruction will have normal or increased numbers of megakaryocytes. A primary marrow disorder may show decreased megakaryocytes or an infiltrar tive process.

【191】1\. Blood product transfusion is an important and frequently life-saving therapy. Adverse reactions to transtusions are common， however， and thus parsimonious use of this intervention is needed. Transfusion reactions are broadly classified as immune and nonimmune. Immune causes include graft versus host disease， post-transfusion thrombocytopenia， alloimmunization， blood pressure instability from anaphylaxis， acute and delayed hemolysis， urticaria， neutrophilic febrile re-actions， and TRALI， a neutrophil-induced lung injury. Nonimmune complica-tions of transfusion include overload (either acute volume expansion or chronic iron overload) and infections.

【192】2\. Graft versus host disease (GVHD) is a rare complication of transfusion re-sulting from transfusion of viable， donor lymphocytes. Transfusion-associated GVHD usually occurs when a patient receives blood from a closely related donor. The donor’s lymphocytes have common antigens and are not recognized as foreign by the recipient. These lymphocytes， however， see the recipient as foreign and proliferate， leading to fulminant multiorgan system failure and death.3. Overload states， either volume or iron， are common nonimmune complica-tions of transfusion. In older patients and patients with cardiac disease， the volume of the transfusion may cause pulmonary edema. This complication can

【193】be avoided by slow infusion or administering a diuretic. Iron overload may occur in patients requiring chronic transfusions. This potentially fatal complica-tion can be prevented with chelation therapy.

【194】_4\._ Thrombocytopenia is a rare consequence of transfusion. It is usually seen in women with a specific platelet antigen-lype， who have had a prior pregnancy. The typical presentation is marked thrombocytopenia occurring several days after a transfusion. Patients spontaneously recover， but steroid therapy or ⅣV immunoglob-ulin may be of benetit.

【21】Spinal dysraphisms. Spinal dysraphisms are divided into open spinal dysraphisms (OSDs)， in which there is exposure of abnormal nervous tissues through a skin defect， and closed spinal dysraphisms (CSDs)， in which there is complete skin coverage of the underly-ing malformation. OSDs basically include open spina bifida， with myelomeningocele， and other rare abnor-malities such as myelocele and hemimyelo (meningo) cele. CSDs will be briefly described at the end of this chapter. The main difference between OSDs and CSDs is that in the former category there is a leakage of CSF within the amniotic cavity and the ensuing hypoten-sion within the subarachnoid spaces triggers a cascade of events that eventually results in the Chiari II malfor-mation \[53\]. In CSDs， there is no loss of CSF and， con-sequently， the cranial anatomy is unremarkable. Their prenatal diagnosis relies only on the direct recognition of the closed spinal defect.

【22】Definitio . The term “spina bifidaais still commonly used as a synonym for spinal dysraphism， although it properly refers to defective fusion of posterior spi-nal bony elements. The terms “spina bifida aperta十节110”or“cystica”and“spina bifida occulta”are used to refer to OSD and CSD， respectively. Myelomeningoceles and myeloceles are characterized by exposure of the placode through a midline defect in the back. In myelomeningo-celes， expansion of the underlying subarachnoid space results in elevation of the placode above the cutaneous surface (open spina bifida with dorsal cyst)， whereas in myeloceles， the placode is flush with the cutaneous surface \[531.

【23】Etiology and pathogenesis. OSDs originate from defec-tive closure of the primary neural tube， which leads to the persistence of a segment of nonneurulated plac-ode. The overall majority of cases are located at the

【24】lumbosacral level， and the placode is terminal. Because neurulation does not occur the cutaneous ectoderm does not detach from the neural ectoderm and remains in a lateral position. This results in a midline skin defect. Therefore， the external surface of the placode is directly visible upon inspection. In an antenatal series，23% of the defects were sacral， 64% lumbosacral，12%thoracolumbar and only 1% cervical.

【25】Ultrasound diagnosis. Until a few decades ago， the prenatal detection rate of spina bifida was relatively low， and was based mainly on serum screening in those countries， such as United States， where this mass screening program was available. The low detection rate for spina bifida on screening US was due to the fact that it is often difficult to obtain a diagnostic view of the fetal spine both in the longitudinal plane and in the axial one； in fact， the fetus often lies with its back along the uterine wall and this hampers the visualization of the fetal spine. Only after the recog-nition that indirect cerebral signs were present in the overwhelming majority of cases of open spina bifida did the detection rate O儿rof this sev CHIere anomaly increasesharply， to reach the current levels of nearly 90%. These indirect signs are related to the fact that in OSDs there is virtually always a Chiari II malforma-tion. This malformation is characterized by a small posterior fossa associated with downward displace-ment of the dysmorphic vermis， the brainstem， and the fourth ventricle into the foramen magnum or even into the cervical spinal canal \[53\]. This cluster of events is triggered by the failed closure of the neuropore， which prevents the physiologic accumulation of fluid in the rhombencephalic vesicle responsible for its physiologic dilatation. As a result， the posterior fossa will be too small to accommodate the growing brainstem and cer-ebellum， and these will herniate through the cervical

【26】canal behind the upper cervical cord. The US diagnosis of the Chiari II malformation is based upon the rec-ognition of a series of signs including： 1) obliterarion of the cisterna magna； 2) dysmorphic and dysplastic cerebellum featuring an abnormal anterior curvature(banana sign)； 3) frontal scalloping (lemon sign). The frontal scalloping (lemon sign) develops early， is incon-stantly present (50% of the cases)， and is lost in most cases by 24 weeks \[51\]. On the contrary， obliteration of the cisterna magna and the cerebellar banana sign are the most sensitive features， with the percentage of false positives being close to zero. These signs can be found from 16 weeks of gestation until term， though it should be considered that the US examination of the fetal posterior fossa is severely hampered in the third trimester by the increased calvarial mineralization.

【27】VM is a relatively late-onset sign. In most cases(70%)， it appears in the in the late second trimester(22-26 weeks.) and worsens thereafter (80%-90%). As mentioned， it is thanks to these indirect cerebral signs that the prenatal detection rate of open spina bifida in western countries has reached figures in the range of 68%-90%， with 68% of the diagnosis before24 weeks of gestation. Once the suspicion of an OSD has been raised because of the recognition of indirect cerebral signs， then a direct approach to the spine is needed， to actually find the level and determine the extent of the spinal defect. It should be pointed out here that the sonographic assessment of the fetal spine is all but difficult even today， being strongly dependent upon the fetal lie. Direct sonographic recognition of the spinal defect requires systematic examination of each neural arch (Figure 2.61)， from the cervical to S. the sacral ones. In particular， the sagittal planes can be used for an overall evaluation of the craniocaudal extension of the defect and to assess the dimensions of the myelomeningocele (Figure 2.61b). On axial views， it is possible to detect the interruption of the cutaneous contour at the level of the affected vertebrae， which will， therefore， show a“C”or“U”configuration， due to absence of the dorsal arches (Figure 2.61a). The cor-onal planes will demonstrate splaying of the lateral processes (Figure 2.61c). The three aspects just men-tioned can be demonstrated advantageously on the same panel of images using the multiplanar display allowed by three-dimensional US. With this approach it is possible to recognize the level and the extent of the spinal defect very easily and at the same time very accurately. This information is of the utmost impor-tance， because the level of the lesion correlates with the extent and the severity of motor and neurofunc-tional dysfunction. These findings can then be advan-tageously employed during the prenatal counseling session with the neurosurgeon. However， it should be

【39】for ventriculoperitoneal shunting and improve motor outcome at 30 months \[56\]. However this represents the first such study， though randomized， showing this improvement at the expense of serious maternal and fetal risks such as premature delivery， abruptio placen-tae， and chorioamnionitis. In addition， only 183 of the initial 1087 women undergoing preliminary screening eventually underwent randomization. Therefore， it is our belief that caution should be aapppplli1e6d in interpret-ing the results of this nonetheless important study， and that we need these data to be supported by other series before accepting prenatal surgery of OSDs as a possibly better alternative to the conventional surgical approach after birth.

Fourteen to Twenty percentage of children with open spina bifida die within the 5 years of life due to， in a certain number of cases， shunt complications. If brainstem disfunction related to Chiari II malformation is present the mortal-ity rate rises to 35-40%.Early neonatal surgery is asso-ciated with the best survival rates， but cannot reduce or prevent disability. A long-term outcome study \[57\] of117 liveborns with spina bifida carried out in the 1970s showed that by a mean age of 30 years， 51% had died. Of the survivors， 84% had a ventricular shunt， 70%had an IQ of 80 or more， 37% lived independently，39% drove a car， 30% could walk more than 50 m，and26% were employed. Normal intelligence was inversely related to presence of hydrocephalus and revision of the ventriculoperitoneal shunt. Infants who do not require ventricular shunting have a mean IQ of 104； if they require it and have no complications， mean IQ is 91； if the shunt needs to be revised， mean IQ is only70. Hence， the presence of hydrocephalus represents a significantly negative prognostic factor； and it has been demonstrated that if fetuses with open spina bifida d l1rreno not have a concurrent hydrocephalus at the time of diagnosis or before 26 weeks of gestation， which is indeed unlikely， there is only a 9% risk for them to develop it later.

【25】**_MANAGEMENT_**

【26】Using only total cholesterol measurements to make man-agement decisions may lead to unwarranted concern or confidence. As discussed above， high-normal levels may be the result of lab error or variation. Approximately 20%of men with confirmed CHD have a cholesterol level be-low 200 mg/dL with an HDLe below 35 mg/dL. It is clear that women with high cholesterol levels， especially those who appear healthy， should not be assumed to be at risk unless confirmed with an associated low HDLc. Men who have a low cholesterol level but either are symp-tomatic for CHD or have significant risk factors should be tested for a low HDLc. In the past， a simple ratio was used between total cholesterol and HDLc， but this may be misleading. For example， two individuals may have a ratio of 5：1. In one individual the total cholesterol is240 mg/dL with an HDLc of 48 mg/dL； the other indi-vidual has a total cholesterol of 150 mg/dL with an HDLo of 30 mg d/L. The second individual. may be at more of a risk than the first based on the low HDLe， especially when other risk factors are added.

【27】Generally， level of risk is known to increase by ap-proximately 3% for each 1% increase in total cholesterol for middle-aged men. Based on the Framingham study， the level of risk is determined by adding point values for each risk factor and using a conversion table to deter-mine the percentage of risk (Table 52--2). These simple calculations may be helpful in defining risk for the patient and illustrate how significant each additional risk factor becomes. In practical application， the level of concern for two patients with a cholesterol level of 240 mg/dL is obviously different. If the patient is a middle-aged man with any risk factors， monitoring levels while applying intervention with diet or medication is warranted， whereas a woman with the same cholesterol level and a high HDLc would warrant less concern.

【7】**SPASTICITY**

【8】This is hypertonicity of the muscle and is almost invari-ably due to a lesion along the pyramidal tract from the spinal cord to the brain. Knowledge of neuroanatomy is extremely useful in developing a differential diagnosis.

【9】Spinal cord： This prompts the recall of space-occupying lesions of the spinal cord， amyotrophic lateral sclero-sis， Friedreich ataxia， transverse myelitis， neurosyphilis， multiple sclerosis， and anterior spinal artery occlusion. Advanced syringomyelia may also be a cause.

【10】Brain stem： Common causes of spasticity originating here include brain stem tumors， hemorrhage， basilar artery thrombosis， multiple sclerosis， bulbar amyotrophic lat-eral sclerosis， encephalomyelitis， and neurosyphilis.

【11】Cerebralhemispheres： Once again， space-occupying lesions are important to recall but hemorrhage， embo-lism， and thrombosis are also prominent causes. In chil-dren it is wise to consider cerebral palsy， encephalitis，

【12】and Schilder disease. There are many degenerative disor-ders of the cerebrum that eventually develop spasticity， but the diagnosis will be well established by that time. Multiple sclerosis that predominantly involves the cere-bral cortex also is unlikely to cause spasticity until late in the course of the disease.

【13】Miscellaneous： The Stiffman syndrome is associated with stiffness of the muscles of the neck， trunk， and extremi-ties. The location of the lesion is unknown.

【14】**Approach to the Diagnosis**

【15】After the level of the lesion is established， an MRI or CT scan of that area can be ordered. A neurologist should be consulted first. A spinal tap will be useful in establishing the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis， encephalitis， and neu-rosyphilis if a space-occupying lesion has been ruled out.

【23】Deformities of the spine are of four types： scoliosis (lat-eral curvature of the spine)， lordosis (lumbar concavity of the spine)， kyphosis (thoracic convexity of the spine or "hunchback")， and kyphoscoliosis (curvature with a“hunchback"). 【48】**SPLENOMEGALY**

【49】The patient is lying on the table and has a palpable mass in the left upper quadrant. The mass has a hard， smooth surface with a notch on the edge and descends on inspira-tion. The patient has an enlarged spleen. What can be done about it? What is causing it?7

【50】The key word is histology. Think about the histologic components： parenchyma， supporting tissue， arteries， veins， and a capsule. What is parenchyma? It is nothing more than the components of the blood： red cells， white cells， lymph tissue， and platelets. Now it is possible to form a differen tial. Increased numbers of red cells recall polycythemia； increased numbers of white cells recall leukemia and infec-tion. Increased lymph tissue suggests Hodgkin lymphoma， whereas increased supporting tissue indicates reticuloen-dotheliosis and acromegaly. Increased vein size occurs in obstruction of the portal vein as in cirrhosis， thrombosis of the portal vein， and CHF. If the artery has a local increase in size， an aneurysm forms， compressing the splenic veins.

【51】A differential is at hand， but it is still incomplete. Now think of physiology. The spleen is a reserve for blood storage. It is also able to form red cells and other compo-nents of the blood when the bone marrow is atrophied， as in extramedullary erythropoiesis. More important， it is involved in the destruction of old or damaged red cells and platelets. Finally， it hypertrophies to fight infection just like the lymph glands. Extramedullary erythropoiesis recalls the splenomegaly of aplastic anemia and myeloid metapla sia， just as destruction or sequestration of cells brings to mind the splenomegaly of hemolytic anemias (e.g.， heredi-tary spherocytosis， malaria， and lupus erythematosus) and thrombocytopenic purpura. The hypertrophy to fight infection or diffuse inflammation of the body should sug gest the splenomegaly of bacterial endocarditis， kala azar infectious mononucleosis， miliary tuberculosis， and rheu-matoid arthritis. Almost anything that causes generalized lymphadenopathy can cause splenomegaly

【52】Only one category of splenomegaly is not brought to mind by this approach， but it is easily remembered because it is an exception-infiltration of inert material. Thus， in gargoylism there is a foreign mucopolysaccharide in the spleen. Numerous mucopolysaccharidoses are now described in the literature. There is a buildup of lipids in the reticuloendotheliosis of Gaucher disease， Niemann-Pick disease， and Hand-Schiiller-Christian disease， but these are intracellular. Amyloid may infiltrate the spleen. Metastatic carcinoma of the spleen is rare.

【53】Table 52 summarizes the above discussion and gives additional causes of splenomegaly to consider in the dif-ferential. One final diagnosis to consider is traumatic splenomegaly.

【54】**Approach to the Diagnosis**

【55】How does one go about pinning down the diagnosis? There are several clinical clues. One looks during the physical examination for jaundice， lymphadenopathy， a rash， sore throat， hepatomegaly， and a positive Rumpel-Leede test. The combination of symptoms and signs will eliminate certain causes and make others more plausible. For exam-ple， splenomegaly with jaundice but no hepatomegaly sug-gests hemolytic anemia. The size of the spleen is also an important differential feature. If the spleen is very large， it should suggest myeloid metaplasia， chronic myelogenous leukemia， Gaucher disease， and kala azar.

【56】The laboratory is the principal aid from this point on. Smears for red cell morphology， malaria， and other para-sites are invaluable. Blood cultures and a lymph node and bone biopsy may be useful. If a specific disease is strongly suspected， consult Appendix A for appropriate tests.

【92】**SPUTUM**

【93】The approach to obtaining a differential is simply to visual-ize the various anatomic components as one travels down the respiratory tree and then to consider the etiologies of each. A nonbloody discharge is almost invariably due to inflammation， infection， or allergy， but a few important exceptions are worth mentioning here.

【94】CHF from any cause (see page 85) produces frothy sputum that is occasionally bloodstained. Many toxic sub-stances can produce severe acute inflammation or mod-erate-to-severe chronic inflammation and fibrosis. Most notable of these are pneumoconiosis， silicosis， berylliosis， and asbestosis. Lipoid pneumonia is mentioned in most

【95】textbooks of differential diagnosis but is seldom seen. Adult respiratory distress syndrome may result from injection of heroin， shock， and septicemia. This condition is associated with frothy sputum also. A few additional exceptions are mentioned as the respiratory tree is traversed.

【96】In diseases of the larynx and trachea， sputum produc-tion is usually scanty， but several viruses (e.g.， influenza) and bacteria (Haemophilus influenzae， pertussis， and diph-theria) may cause a productive sputum. Allergic laryngotra-cheitis does not usually produce sputum.

【97】The bronchi may be inflamed by viruses (e.g.， influ-enza and measles)， bacteria， and particularly by bronchial asthma. In bacterial infection， the sputum is usually yel-low， whereas in bronchial asthma it is white， thick， and mucoid. Chronic bronchitis is usually associated with ciga-rette smoking or exposure to some other irritating inhalant(such as silicon dioxide). Bronchiectasis may result from acute or chronic bronchitis， or from a congenital lesion(e.g.， cystic fibrosis). The sputum in this condition is espe-cially copious (1 cup \[240 mL\] or more per day) and sep-arates into three layers： a frothy layer (saliva)； a greenish layer (white cells and bacteria)； and a brown layer (yellow bodies， elastic fibers， or Dittrich plugs).

【98】The bronchioles and alveoli are the seat of numerous forms of pneumonia. The most common are bacterial， particularly Streptococcus pneumoniae， but staphylococcal，

【99】●FIGURE 9Splenomegaly.

【100】Klebsiella， and H. influenzae forms are not unusual. Gram negative pneumonia is more common in hospitalized patients， especially those who are debilitated or those who have preexisting lung disease or malignancy. Viral pneumo-nias are also frequent and include psittacosis， mycoplasma， and even influenza or measles.

【101】One cannot bypass either the miliary or the cavitary form of tuberculosis as a frequent cause of a chronic persistent

【102】cough that produces grayish yellow sputum. Lung abscesses are important causes of nonbloody sputum； the sputum is usually foul smelling (one can barely stand to walk in the room) because of the many anaerobes in the abscess. Histoplasmosis and other fungi must be looked for.

【103】Allergic and autoimmune diseases that involve the alve-oli and may produce nonbloody sputum include Loeffler pneumonitis， Wegener granuloma， rheumatoid arthritis，

【104】scleroderma， and lupus erythematosus. Even rheumatic fever can produce a pneumonitis. A more extensive display of the conditions that may produce nonbloody sputum is demonstrated in Table 53.

【105】**Approach to the Diagnosis**

【106】Obviously， the approach to the diagnosis begins with exami-nation of the sputum. In acute cases， a Gram stain often shows pneumococci or other bacteria. The laboratory should exam-ine a 24-hour sputum for Curschmann spirals (of bronchial asthma)， eosinophils， and elastic fibers， but so should the physician (to differentiate bronchiectasis and lung abscess).

【107】The chest x-ray (posterior anterior and both laterals) plus proper examination of the sputum and culture (rou-tine and acid-fast bacillus \[AFB\]) are usually all that are necessary. Spirometry and a circulation time will help rule out CHF. Bronchoscopy， bronchography， and lung scans may be necessary in chronic or subacute cases. Repeated cultures and smears are often rewarding. Lung aspiration and biopsy may also be necessary.

【123】**STOOL COLOR CHANGES**

【124】What may be black and white and red all over? The answer is not the newspaper but the pathologic changes in the stool. A black stool is usually melena (see page 208)， but do not be fooled by iron ingestion or the bismuth in a commonly used antacid. A white or light-colored stool is most com-monly found following the ingestion of a barium test meal， but the clay-colored stool of obstructive jaundice suggests the most important disease to be considered. The stool is light yellow to foamy in celiac disease. In mucous colitis， a large cast of white mucus (sometimes 6 to 10 in \[15.2 to25.4 cm\] long) may be described as a white "stool." A red stool signifies blood from the lower bowel (see page 367) in most cases， but ingestion of red beets is not an uncom-iion catise.

【125】The riddle mentioned above forms a key to remember-ing the causes of aberrations in stool color. Another method is to apply biochemistry. The normal color of the stool is due to the pigment urobilinogen. Color changes may result from a decrease in or absence of this pigment (obstructive

【126】jaundice)， from an increase (hemolytic anemia) or the addition of another pigment (hemoglobin in melena)， and finally from the addition of another substance such as mucus in mucous colitis， fat in celiac disease， and bismuth in antacid ingestion.

【1】Patients with venous claudication usually have varicose veins. Occasionally they can identify a tender point in the calf， but examination is not revealing. These patients should exercise to the point of discomfort， at which time a group of varices may be noted. Venography may be required for diagnosis.

【2】The classic findings in patients with thrombophlebitis are swelling and a measurable increase in calf circumference in comparison with

【3】the opposite side. The clinician can often palpate a tender cordlike vein between the heads of the gastrocnemius muscle. The patient may have dilation of other veins， edema， erythema， and Homans’ sign. These findings are variable and not always reliable for the diagnosis of thrombophlebitis. Inflation of a sphygmomanometer around each calf until pain is produced is a sensitive test. The most important tests are venography and duplex Doppler ultrasonography.

【4】Because cellulitis of the calf can mimic thrombophlebitis， the two conditions must be differentiated. In cellulitis， the pain is described as being on the surface， no palpable cord is present， and Homans’ sign is absent. Careful examination reveals that pain is induced by light palpation rather than deep palpation over the course of the vein. Likewise， the area of erythema is more clearly demarcated， occasionally with an associated open wound. An inflated sphygmomanometer requires high pressure to reproduce the pain of cellulitis， and often there is no difference in pressure between the two calves. These findings contrast with those reported in patients with thrombophlebitis. Because thrombophlebitis may coexist with a popliteal (Baker's) cyst， venous Doppler ultrasonography should be performed in all patients with popliteal cysts.
